clue.text: Poet’s occasional work about University church (7)

explanation.surface: A poet picking up casual work for a university chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasional work' looks like a dig at how little a poet writes, and it is really the charwoman's noun: a stint of odd jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in verse and is the poet English literature starts with, so 'Poet' names him by his trade.

indicators.note: Wrapping one thing about another puts it round the outside, so the short pieces land in the middle of the longer one.

blocks.note: a char is an odd job done now and then, the charwoman's word for casual domestic work
U is the standard short form for university
CE, the Church of England, is the crossword's church

clue.text: Stop copper taking on aggressive salesman (3,3)

explanation.surface: A policeman signing up a pushy salesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is the metal here, not the policeman the salesman in the surface is asking you to picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut out is what an engine does when it stops dead, so 'Stop' is the intransitive verb — quit, pack in — rather than an order.

indicators.note: To take something on is to take it aboard, so what follows is added onto the letters already there.

blocks.note: CU is the chemical symbol for copper
a tout is the one who pushes tickets at you outside the ground

clue.text: Information spiking a US lawyer’s expected work (6)

explanation.surface: A leak of information landing on an American prosecutor's list of jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiking' reads as a newsdesk word — a story spiked is a story killed — and the instruction it carries is impaling one word on another.
explanation.definitionFit: Agenda is Latin for 'things to be done', so it names the work a meeting is expected to get through, item by item.

indicators.note: To spike a thing is to drive a point straight through it, so these letters end up pushed into the middle of the words beside them.

blocks.note: the clue's own indefinite article, taken across as a letter
gen is British slang for the information you need — 'give me the gen' — out of forces use
DA is the District Attorney, the prosecutor in an American court

clue.text: Add something to study, with a lot of attempts to suppress objection (10)

explanation.surface: Someone told to add to their research while an objection is shouted down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is a verb, not a room, and the objection is clued by the one word everybody raises an objection with.
explanation.definitionFit: To contribute is to add something to a common pot — money, an idea, a chapter — so the definition is the plain action the verb names.

indicators.note: A lot of a word is most but not all of it, so the last letter is left behind.
To suppress something is to hold it down out of sight, and out of sight here means inside the letters that close over it.

blocks.note: to con a text is to study it closely, an old sense crosswords keep alive
attempts are tries, and a lot of that word is all of it bar the final letter
the word an objection begins with: 'but…'

clue.text: Take another exam? Refuse, dismissing an opening from school (5)

explanation.surface: A candidate refuses, and a place at the school is taken off the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is the verb stressed on its second syllable, not the rubbish a school might have cleared, and 'an opening' is one letter rather than a vacancy.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is the paper you take again after failing it, and the question mark admits the definition is a description rather than a synonym.

indicators.note: To dismiss someone is to send them away, so the letter named next leaves the word altogether.
An opening is where a thing starts, so this asks for the letter its word opens with.

blocks.note: to resist an order is to refuse it, and this is the word before anything is taken out
school opens with S, and that is the letter dismissed

clue.text: Minion whips another minion endlessly (4-3)

explanation.surface: One underling flogging another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minion' is used twice on purpose, once as definition and once as the chess pawn, and the answer comes from the fable of the monkey using the cat's paw to rake chestnuts out of the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's-paw is someone used as a tool by another, which is a minion in the exact sense of a dupe sent to do the dirty work.

indicators.note: A word taken endlessly has its end knocked off, so the final letter never arrives.

blocks.note: the cat-o'-nine-tails was the navy's flogging whip, so whips are cats
a pawn is the lowest piece on the board and the errand-runner of the metaphor, and its end is dropped

clue.text: Islands’ postal service getting a source of protection (5,4)

explanation.surface: An island post office throwing in something that keeps you safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words that read as one idea — the islands' mail — turn out to be separate pieces, and the second is the armourer's spelling, from the French maille, a ring of mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain mail is the linked metal mesh a soldier wore into battle, so the definition is protection in the literal, wearable sense.

blocks.note: islands strung out in a line are called a chain, as the Hawaiian ones are
the mail is what the postal service carries, and in Britain what it is called

clue.text: What actor seeks has turned up – something on the stage? (4)

explanation.surface: An actor's hoped-for part has finally come along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' does both jobs at once: arrived, which is the surface, and reversed, which is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap is the trapdoor built into a stage floor for a demon king to rise through, so the definition points at theatre carpentry.

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so a piece that has turned up is read from the bottom towards the top and arrives backwards.

blocks.note: an actor is after a part, and those four letters climb the grid, so they arrive the other way round

clue.text: Indicates remaining bits under computer socket (8)

explanation.surface: Spare scraps of hardware sitting beneath a computer's socket.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are computing words on the surface, and the definition is the one thing here with nothing to do with machines: an omen.
explanation.definitionFit: To portend is to be a sign of what is coming, which is what 'indicates' means when a thing rather than a person does it.

indicators.note: This entry runs down the page, so the piece said to be under the other is written below it, second.

blocks.note: a port is the socket you plug a cable into on the side of a machine
the bits left over at the finish are the ends, as in odds and ends

clue.text: No great confusion, we hear, when most are at work (8)

explanation.surface: No great muddle, apparently, on the days when most people are working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No great' has to be heard as a single adjective before the sound-alike will work, which is why neither half looks anything like the word it came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Weekdays are Monday to Friday, so the definition names them by the one thing nearly everybody does on them.

indicators.note: What follows is reported by ear, so it is the noise of the words that counts and not their spelling.

blocks.note: something no great shakes is weak, and that noise is written down this other way
the confusion you are left in is a daze, and said aloud it is spelt like this

clue.text: Male accessory – popular marketing move (3-2)

explanation.surface: Something a man wears with a shirt, and a bright idea for shifting more of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does all the hiding: it reads as a pause between two thoughts and is really the join between two pieces of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-in is the mug or the toy sold on the back of a film, so 'marketing move' is the trade's own description of it.

blocks.note: the strip of silk knotted at a man's collar
what is popular this season is in — the crossword's usual two letters for fashionable

clue.text: Rakes active around a block turned over in prehistoric site (5,4)

explanation.surface: Rakish idlers busying themselves around an overturned stone at an ancient settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: Skara Brae is the Neolithic village on Orkney that a storm stripped bare in 1850, and 'Rakes' is the old word for dissolute men — nothing here is a garden tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Skara Brae is a 5,000-year-old stone village on Orkney, so 'prehistoric site' is the plain archaeological label for it.

indicators.note: An active thing will not sit still, and letters that will not sit still come back in some other order.
What goes around a thing encloses it, so these letters open up and take the next ones inside.
Something turned over ends up facing the other way, so those letters are read from the back.

blocks.note: the five letters of the clue's first word, resettled before anything goes inside them
a block of wood or stone is a bar, and it is the bar alone that turns, with the 'a' left standing in front

clue.text: Get where sports ground security might not find you? (10)

explanation.surface: A tip on where to hide from the stewards at a football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' is the definition and the only part of the clue not about football; everything after it is one picture, a hiding place a steward would walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: To understand something is to get it, in the everyday 'I get it' sense of a penny dropping rather than of obtaining anything.

blocks.note: the place a sweep of the ground would miss is beneath something, and beneath is this word

clue.text: Stop, exhausted, toppling over, nothing less (3)

explanation.surface: An exhausted walker halting, keeling over, with nothing left to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing less' reads as 'nothing short of' and is an instruction to subtract: nothing is the round letter, and out it comes.
explanation.definitionFit: To end is to stop — a play ends, a road ends — the intransitive verb rather than the noun the surface's exhausted walker suggests.

indicators.note: Something that topples over lands the other way up, so those letters are read backwards.
'Less' is doing arithmetic, not comparison: what it names is subtracted from what has been built.

blocks.note: someone exhausted is done in, and those four letters are tipped over to read the other way
nothing is O, the letter shaped like a zero, and it is the one taken away

clue.text: Pretty US lawyer, busy imprisoning Republican (10)

explanation.surface: A hard-working American lawyer with a Republican locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' stands exactly where an adjective describing the lawyer would stand, which is what makes it so easy to read as part of the picture instead of as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive means good-looking, and 'Pretty' is the everyday word for it — the adjective, not 'pretty' meaning fairly.

indicators.note: To imprison someone is to shut them inside walls, so the letter named is locked in between the pieces either side.

blocks.note: an American attorney is shortened to att, as on a law firm's letterhead
R is the letter printed beside an American politician's name when they sit on that side
somebody busy is active, out doing things

clue.text: Leads by running around region unthinkingly? (12)

explanation.surface: A front-runner building a lead by jogging round the district without thinking about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads' looks like the standing instruction to take first letters; here it is ordinary fodder, and 'running' is what unsettles it.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a thing abstractedly is to do it with your mind elsewhere, which is 'unthinkingly' in the absent sense rather than the stupid one.

indicators.note: Ink runs, dye runs: anything running spreads where it likes, and letters given that freedom settle somewhere new.
What is placed around a thing wraps right round it, so the shuffled letters open to take the next word inside.

blocks.note: the seven letters of the clue's first two words, set down in a different order
a tract is a stretch of country — a tract of moorland — so it is a region

clue.text: Those people seen around shady area where New York drunks gather (3,6)

explanation.surface: Locals loitering round a disreputable patch of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady' is the trap: it wants to mean disreputable, to match the drunks, and it means full of leaves — a bower is a garden arbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bowery is the Manhattan street that became America's byword for flophouses and skid row, so the definition names it by its old reputation.

indicators.note: To be seen around a place is to be all over it, so this word goes right round the one beside it.

blocks.note: those people over there are they, and the word splits to let something in
a bower is the leafy shelter in a garden, shady in the literal sense

clue.text: Flush sewage after Australian takes over leadership (8)

explanation.surface: Sewage flushed away once an Australian has taken charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flush' is the definition and it means rolling in money, not the lavatory flush that the sewage beside it is pushing you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody flush is well supplied with cash for the moment, which is what affluent means: wealthy, in funds.

indicators.note: Taking over the leadership is stepping into the top job, so this letter replaces the one standing at the front.

blocks.note: effluent is the waste liquid a treatment works discharges, the technical word for sewage
A is the short form for Australian, and it is the letter moving in

clue.text: Medic to leave, upset, with woozy head? It’s the port (8)

explanation.surface: A doctor walking out in a huff with a thick head, and the port wine gets the blame.

explanation.definitionFit: Drogheda is a port on the Boyne in County Louth, so the definition is the plain geographical label and not the fortified wine.

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so a piece that is upset is tipped over and read from the bottom upwards.
Someone woozy can keep nothing straight, and letters that cannot be kept straight come out in another order.

blocks.note: DR is the doctor's title, the medic's two letters

clue.text: Naval leader: source for support for idle tars, possibly (5,3,4)

explanation.surface: A fund set up to keep unemployed sailors going.
explanation.walkthrough: A tar is a sailor, so the surface's men out of work and the definition's admiral are the same trade seen from opposite ends of the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The First Sea Lord is the admiral who runs the Royal Navy, so 'Naval leader' is his job description almost word for word.

indicators.note: A source is where a thing starts, so this asks for the letter the next word starts with.

clue.text: Delicate sex? Mostly safe to accept that (6)

explanation.surface: The delicate sex, and whether it is still safe to accept the description.

explanation.definitionFit: Petite describes a woman as small and finely built, which is 'delicate' in the sense of slight rather than fragile.

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the final letter, so that letter is left off.

blocks.note: a peter is a safe in old criminal slang — cracking one is blowing a peter — and most of it stops short of the last letter

clue.text: Immature supporter interrupting international (6)

definitions.note: 'Immature' is an adjective where the answer is usually a noun; the setter is allowed it because the noun works attributively too — an infant industry is an immature one.

explanation.surface: A very young fan barging into an international fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' in a crossword is usually a bra or a pillar, and here it is the ordinary one: the fan standing in the crowd that 'international' has already put you in.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is at the earliest stage of growing, so 'immature' names the state exactly: not yet grown rather than childish in behaviour.

indicators.note: To interrupt is to cut in part-way through, so this piece breaks into the middle of the word beside it.

blocks.note: INT is the standard short form for international, as on a fixture list

clue.text: Taking considerable time, missing new record (3)

explanation.surface: A runner too slow to break the new record.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an athlete falling short, and the definition is the other kind of record entirely: the written account kept day by day.
explanation.definitionFit: A log is the running written record a ship or a pilot keeps, so 'record' is the noun in its filing sense, not a disc or a best time.

blocks.note: a job that takes considerable time is a long one, and this is the word before the cut

clue.text: Caught one to create mascara? (3,4-2)

explanation.surface: The bass thumping in zone 2 brought back memories of a district on a party island.

explanation.surface: An ageing actor having a go at staging some Shakespeare.

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's plays divide into comedies, histories and tragedies, so the definition names one of those categories by example.

clue.text: Finished end of route at gorge (7)

explanation.surface: Reaching the far end of the road at a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gorge' is a verb here, and the surface spends its whole length making it a landscape feature at the end of a walk.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to stuff yourself well past the point of sense, which is what overeating is; the ravine is the surface's other noun.

indicators.note: The end of a word is its last letter, and that single letter is all this takes.

blocks.note: when a match is finished it is over
